annotatedSteps.description: Assume contradiction and form algebraic relation
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: × Invalid method: calculating a few decimal places does not prove a decimal is non-terminating and non-repeating.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking: Let us assume, to the contrary, that 1/√5 is rational. Then 1/√5 = a/b, where a and b are co-prime integers and b ≠ 0.

annotatedSteps.studentWork:
The decimal expansion of 1/√5 is non-terminating and non-repeating.
A rational number always has a terminating or repeating decimal expansion.
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: × Cannot claim non-terminating non-repeating behavior without a rigorous algebraic proof.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking: Rearranging 1/√5 = a/b gives √5 = b/a. Since a and b are integers, b/a is rational, which implies √5 is rational.

annotatedSteps.studentWork: ∴ 1/√5 is an irrational number. Hence proved.
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: × Conclusion follows from an invalid method.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking: This contradicts the fact that √5 is irrational. This contradiction arose because of our incorrect assumption. Hence, 1/√5 is irrational.

teacherNote: Marked against: Assume to the contrary that 1/√5 is rational / writing 1/√5 = a/b where a and b are co-prime integers (b ≠ 0) (1); Rearrange to express √5 = b/a and state that b/a is rational since a / b are integers (1); State the contradiction to the fact that √5 is irrational and conclude that 1/√5 is irrational (1). Irrationality cannot be proved by showing a few decimal places, as finite digits cannot demonstrate non-terminating and non-repeating behavior. Use the standard proof by contradiction: assume 1/√5 = a/b (co-prime integers) and show that this falsely implies √5 is rational. This method does not work in general, so the working built on it cannot earn method marks — use a method that holds in every case.
